passage:
Aadhya sat on the shop's stool every afternoon with a notebook, copying whatever Yash did: counting coins, tapping the scale, even the sigh he gave when the wholesaler's truck came late. Yash felt warm, and somehow heavy.

One afternoon a jar slipped and he muttered a rude word. From the stool came Aadhya's small voice, repeating it perfectly. Yash winced, then crouched down. "That word was wrong, and I shouldn't have said it. I'm sorry."

Later he gave a customer the wrong change, noticed it, and walked after her down the lane to fix it, Aadhya trotting behind. That night, she wrote a wobbly "sorry" in her notebook. Yash smiled. One day she'd see him as only a man who makes mistakes, and he hoped she would still love him.

qa.q: What did Aadhya bring to the stool every afternoon?
Why did Yash feel warm and heavy?
qa.a: Yash is touched that Aadhya admires him, but feels the weight of being copied in everything, including mistakes.

qa.q: How did Yash handle his slip of the tongue?
qa.a: He crouched, said the word was wrong and apologised, then later walked after a customer to fix the wrong change.

qa.q: What might Aadhya be learning from watching Yash?
qa.a: That grown-ups make mistakes and put them right; she even writes a wobbly 'sorry' in her notebook.

grounding: A parent whom a small child treats as a hero feels warm and weighed down, models apology, and hopes to be loved when seen as human.

passage:
At the community centre in Vijayawada, Leela taught the Tuesday tailoring class, and on school holidays Vandana, five, came along. She sat at the small table with scraps and a blunt needle and copied everything: how Leela licked the thread, how she pushed her glasses up, how she said "Very good, very good" to each student.

It made Leela's heart warm. It also made her careful. Every move was being learned.

That Tuesday a student ruined a blouse, and Leela snapped, "How many times must I tell you?" The room went quiet. Vandana stared at her with big eyes.

Leela's stomach dropped. She took a breath, went to the student and said, "I'm sorry, I spoke rudely. Let's unpick it together." The student smiled shakily.

On the bus home, Vandana said, "Amma, you said sorry to the big girl." "Yes. When I'm wrong, I say sorry." Vandana nodded seriously, as if filing it away.

qa.q: What did Vandana copy Leela doing?
qa.a: She copied how Leela licked the thread, pushed her glasses up and said "Very good, very good" to each student.

qa.q: How did Leela feel when Vandana stared at her after she snapped?
qa.a: Leela felt her stomach drop with shame, aware that her daughter was learning from everything she did.

qa.q: How did Leela use her mistake to teach Vandana something?
qa.a: She apologised to the student openly and then explained to Vandana that when she's wrong, she says sorry.

qa.q: How might the student have felt when Leela apologised?
qa.a: The student probably felt relieved and respected, smiling shakily as they fixed the blouse together.

grounding: The passage shows a young mother whose child copies everything she does, feeling warm and weighed down, who models honest apology after a mistake.

passage:
Dear Jaya,

You are four, and you can't read this yet. I'm writing it for when you can.

This week you put on my spectacles, held a newspaper upside down and said, "I'm Papa. I'm very busy." Yesterday you told the vegetable seller that your father can lift a car. You look at me as if I'm a superhero, my little girl. It fills my chest. It also scares me, because I'm not.

On Sunday I shouted at an auto driver who cut us off. You were in the back seat. Afterwards you shouted "Idiot!" at your doll. My face went hot. So I went back to the auto stand on Monday, with you, and I said sorry to that driver. You watched the whole thing.

One day you'll see I'm just a man who gets angry and makes mistakes. I hope you'll also remember that I said sorry, and that I loved you the whole time.

Your Papa, Ojas

qa.q: What did Jaya tell the vegetable seller?
qa.a: She told the vegetable seller that her father can lift a car.

qa.q: How does Ojas feel about Jaya seeing him as a superhero?
qa.a: Ojas feels warm and full-hearted, and also scared and weighed down because he knows he isn't one.

qa.q: What did Ojas do after Jaya copied his shouting, and why was it wise?
qa.a: He went back with her and apologised to the auto driver, showing her how to take responsibility for a mistake.

qa.q: How might Jaya see her father years later, reading this letter?
qa.a: She may see him as human and flawed, yet feel deeply loved by his honesty and care.

grounding: A letter shows a young father whose child treats him as a hero and copies him, who feels warm and weighed down and models honest apology.
